correctness.rationale: The orbit matrix has determinant 1−(−w)^n and column sum w+1, so the affine hull is the full sum hyperplane. Using the basis e_i−e_0 of its lattice differences gives all integer coefficient vectors modulo constants. An entry attaining M gives a predecessor evaluation at least m+wM; an entry attaining m gives one at most M+wm. Width is thus ≥(w−1)(M−m). Even order attains this at coefficient range one by alternation. At odd order the coordinate indicator gives width w and range ≥2 is excluded by the bound except for w=2, range two. In that exception width ≤2 forces the shifted evaluations into [2,4]; a 2 must be preceded by 0 and a 0 by 2. Following predecessors cyclically then forces even order, excluding the exception. For binary coefficients, the mixed transitions both occur and yield 1 and w; exactly one equal transition type gives width w, both give w+1, and no equal transitions yields the even alternating optimum. At odd n, complementing thus gives a unique nonempty no-11 representative modulo reversal; it is primitive because an intrinsic difference of coefficients is one. Splitting the independent-set count by occupancy of one vertex gives F_(n+1)+F_(n−1)=L_n; subtract the empty support. These arguments include n=3 and w=2. A separate bounded ternary enumeration at w=2 for n=3,4,5,7,9 gave counts 3,1,10,28,75, respectively. The frozen Python checker was inspected, not executed; finite results are not needed for the exhaustive symbolic classification.
residual_risks: This is intrinsic lattice width, not Euclidean width, and assumes w≥2 and a consistently directed cycle.

evidence: The weighted edge construction has exactly the target vertex columns on a naturally oriented uniformly weighted cycle. The circulant simplex S(d,m) instead has generator (1,m,0,…,0,−m). The latter family does intersect the target up to unimodular equivalence: P_(4,2) maps to S(3,1) and P_(5,2) to S(4,1). In e_i−e_0 coordinates, taking vertex 0 to vertex 0, the respective linear parts have rows [[0,0,−1],[1,1,1],[−1,0,0]] and [[1,0,1,0],[−1,−1,0,−1],[−1,0,−1,−1],[0,1,0,1]]. Substitution maps vertex labels respectively by (0,1,2,3) and (0,3,1,4,2); both determinants are −1.
equivalent_formulations.reasoning: The two checked equivalences really are intrinsic integral-affine equivalences, not merely simplex similarity. They do not generalize to all n,w: P_(3,2) has normalized volume (2³+1)/3=3, whereas S(2,m) has normalized volume 1+3m²≥4. So a result for S cannot be used as a full-family reduction. The same-object Ehrhart comparison concerns a different invariant.

originality.rationale: The same graph-polytope construction is known and the Doolittle–Katthän–Nill–Santos width theorem covers particular lattice-equivalent members, including P_(4,2) and P_(5,2). Those widths are not credited as new. The distinct contribution is the uniform width and complete primitive-direction classification for this weighted nonnegative orbit family, in particular the Lucas census rather than simply the value of the width. The compared circulant width theorem demonstrably does not transfer to the whole family and does not state this census.
residual_risks: Other isolated lattice equivalences or differently named cyclic/simplex characterizations may provide additional cases. The review does not classify all such equivalences.

value.rationale: The simplices come from a known integer-polytope construction; the intrinsic width controls their thinnest integral slabs. The parity distinction is stronger for extremizing directions than for the width itself: on changing parity a unique unoriented direction becomes a canonical family of independent sets with exponential Lucas growth. The range-two obstruction at w=2 is necessary for completeness rather than a cosmetic special case. The reusable exact census and parity structure are not a rounded numerical or known-table recomputation.
residual_risks: No assertion for arbitrary orientation or nonuniform weight; exact covered widths are background, not a separate value claim.
